## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97665.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97665.3.sa1)

Summary:

Dr. Santamaria's group previously utilized antigen-specific nanomedicines to induce immune tolerance in treating autoimmune diseases. The success of this therapeutic strategy has been linked to expanded regulatory mechanisms, particularly the role of T-regulatory type-1 (TR1) cells. However, the differentiation program of TR1 cells remained largely unclear. Previous work from the authors suggested that TR1 cells originate from T follicular helper (TFH) cells. In the current study, the authors aimed to investigate the epigenetic mechanisms underlying the transdifferentiation of TFH cells into IL-10-producing TR1 cells. Specifically, they sought to determine whether this process involves extensive chromatin remodeling or is driven by pre-existing epigenetic modifications. Their goal was to understand the transcriptional and epigenetic changes facilitating this transition and to explore the potential therapeutic implications of manipulating this pathway.

The authors successfully demonstrated that the TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process is driven by pre-existing epigenetic modifications rather than extensive new chromatin remodeling. The comprehensive transcriptional and epigenetic analyses provide robust evidence supporting their conclusions.

Strengths:

(1) The study employs a broad range of bulk and single-cell transcriptional and epigenetic tools, including RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and DNA methylation analysis. This comprehensive approach provides a detailed examination of the epigenetic landscape during the TFH-to-TR1 transition.

(2) The use of high-throughput sequencing technologies and sophisticated bioinformatics analyses strengthens the foundation for the conclusions drawn.

(3) The data generated can serve as a valuable resource for the scientific community, offering insights into the epigenetic regulation of T cell plasticity.

(4) The findings have significant implications for developing new therapeutic strategies for autoimmune diseases, making the research highly relevant and impactful.

Weaknesses:

(1) While the study focuses on transcriptional and epigenetic analyses, the authors are currently undertaking efforts to validate these findings functionally. Ongoing research aims to further explore the roles of key transcription factors in the TFH-to-TR1 transition, reflecting the authors' commitment to building on the insights gained from this study.

(2) The identification of key transcription factors and epigenetic marks is a strong foundation for future work. The authors are actively investigating how these factors drive chromatin remodeling, which will enhance the mechanistic understanding of the TFH-to-TR1 process in future studies.

(3) Although the study provides a valuable snapshot of the epigenetic landscape, the authors are pursuing additional research to assess the dynamics of these changes over time. These ongoing efforts will contribute to a deeper understanding of the stability and progression of the observed epigenetic modifications.

Comments on revised version:

The authors have effectively discussed and addressed all previously raised questions. There are no further concerns.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97665.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97665.3.sa2)

Summary:

This study, based on their previous findings that TFH cells can be converted into TR1 cells, conducted a highly detailed and comprehensive epigenetic investigation to answer whether TR1 differentiation from TFH is driven by epigenetic changes. Their evidence indicated that the downregulation of TFH-related genes during the TFH to TR1 transition depends on chromatin closure, while the upregulation of TR1-related genes does not depend on epigenetic changes.

Strengths:

A significant advantage of their approach lies in its detailed and comprehensive assessment of epigenetics. Their analysis of epigenetics covers chromatin open regions, histone modifications, DNA methylation, and using both single-cell and bulk techniques to validate their findings. As for their results, observations from different epigenetic perspectives mutually supported each other, lending greater credibility to their conclusions. This study effectively demonstrates that 1. the TFH-to-TR1 differentiation process is associated with massive closure of OCRs, and 2. the TR1-poised epigenome of TFH cells is a key enabler of this transdifferentiation process. Considering the extensive changes in epigenetic patterns involved in other CD4+ T lineage commitment processes, the similarity between TFH and TR1 in their epigenetics is intriguing.

They performed correlation analysis to answer the association between "pMHC-NP-induced epigenetic change" and "gene expression change in TR1". Also, they have made their raw data publicly available, providing a comprehensive epigenomic database of pMHC-NP induced TR1 cells. This will serve as a valuable reference for future research.

Weaknesses:

A major limitation is that this study heavily relies on a premise from the previous studies performed by the same group on pMHC-NP-induced T cell responses. This significantly limits the relevance of their conclusion to a broader perspective. Specifically, differential OCRs between Tet+ and naïve T cells were limited to only 821, as compared to 10,919 differential OCRs between KLH-TFH and naïve T cells (Fig. 2A), indicating that the precursors and T cell clonotypes that responded to pMHC-NP were extremely limited. I acknowledge that this limitation has been added and discussed in the Discussion section of the revised manuscript.

results.result: The TFH-to-TR1 cell transdifferentiation process involves massive chromatin closure, with most open chromatin regions (OCRs) in TR1 cells already present in TFH cells, and minimal generation of new OCRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C44, C59-C61, C68, C139-C140 collectively demonstrate through single-cell and bulk ATACseq data (Figures 1C, 2A) that TFH-to-TR1 conversion involves extensive chromatin closure with limited new OCR formation. The scMultiome and bulk ATACseq analyses consistently show that the vast majority of OCRs remaining in TR1 cells were already open at the TFH stage, supporting the conclusion of massive chromatin contraction during transdifferentiation.

results.result: Chromatin closure during TFH-to-TR1 conversion is strongly associated with gene downregulation, with 87.2% of differentially expressed genes being downregulated and 94% of genes with closed chromatin regions showing decreased expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65, C72, C74 are supported by scRNAseq data from the scMultiome dataset (Figure 1D-E) and bulk RNAseq/ATACseq analyses (Figure 2C), showing statistically significant associations (p=8.25e-14, p=1.38e-08) between chromatin closure and gene downregulation. The data consistently demonstrate that massive chromatin closure accompanies extensive gene silencing during the TFH-to-TR1 transition.

results.result: TR1-associated genes, including Il10, are epigenetically poised for expression at the TFH cell stage, being accessible, hypomethylated, and enriched for H3K27ac-marked active enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C8, C45, C47, C94, C141 are supported by comprehensive epigenetic analyses including ATACseq, ChIPseq (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac), and methylation data (Figures 3, 4, 6C). The data show that genes upregulated during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation have nearly identical histone modification patterns and methylation status in both TFH and TR1 cells, indicating epigenetic poising at the TFH stage.

results.result: TR1-associated genes are closed and hypermethylated in conventional T cells (Tconv), but share remarkably similar methylation patterns between TFH and TR1 cells, with the methylation status already imprinted at the TFH stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C46, C99, C108, C142 are supported by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data (Figure 4) showing that 87.5% of genes with accessible chromatin in both TFH and TR1 cells have similar methylation status (p<1.85e-5). The data demonstrate that while these genes are hypermethylated in Tconv cells, they are hypomethylated in both TFH and TR1 cells, indicating methylation imprinting at the TFH stage.

results.result: Active enhancers linked to genes upregulated at the TR1 stage are enriched for binding sites for TFH-associated transcription factors TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF, with ~61% of these TF-binding enhancers already present in TFH cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C133-C137 are supported by integrated analysis of ChIPseq data for TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF with active enhancer predictions (Figure 7C, Figure 6C). The data show that 34.4%, 66.3%, and 70.1% of active enhancers have TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF binding sites respectively, with ~61% present in TFH cells vs. <2% in Tconv cells (p<3.03e-8), indicating these sites are likely occupied at the TFH stage.

results.result: The TR1 gene expression program is genetically imprinted at the TFH cell stage, with TFH cells being epigenetically poised to become TR1 cells, representing a key enabler of the transdifferentiation process.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C48, C138, C144 represent the main conclusion of the study, supported by the comprehensive integration of all epigenetic data (chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, DNA methylation, and active enhancers). The collective evidence from multiple orthogonal approaches consistently demonstrates that TR1-associated genes are epigenetically marked for expression at the TFH stage, supporting the concept of genomic imprinting as a key enabler of transdifferentiation.

results.result: For genes with chromatin regions that remain accessible during TFH-to-TR1 conversion, differential gene expression is not correlated with changes in chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, or active enhancer distribution, suggesting regulation by other factors such as transcription factor availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67, C104, C109, C111-C112, C119, C122, C129 are supported by statistical analyses showing no significant correlations (p=0.92, p=0.76, p=1) between differential gene expression and various epigenetic marks for genes with shared chromatin accessibility. The data from Figures 1F, 4E, 6B, 7B consistently demonstrate that differential expression of these genes is dissociated from epigenetic modifications, supporting the conclusion that other factors (e.g., TF availability) regulate their expression.

results.result: Transcription factor-coding genes that are downregulated during TFH-to-TR1 conversion close a significant number of open chromatin regions (13/29 downregulated vs. 4/38 upregulated, p<0.0001), while upregulation of TF-coding genes is largely dissociated from epigenetic marks.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by integrated analysis of scMultiome and epigenetic data (Figure 5) showing a statistically significant association (p<0.0001) between TF gene downregulation and chromatin closure. The data demonstrate that loss of TFH-associated TF expression is driven in part by chromatin remodeling, while TR1-promoting TF upregulation occurs independently of the epigenetic marks studied.

results.result: Most genes that remain open during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation harbor active enhancers that are shared between TFH and TR1 cells (89.6%, p<2.2e-16), with 68.9% of these genes being downregulated in TR1 cells despite maintaining active enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118, C120-C121 are supported by integrated ATACseq and H3K27ac ChIPseq analyses (Figure 6A-B) showing that the Tet+ pool shares significantly more active enhancers with TFH cells (80.2%) than with Tconv cells (55.5%, p<2.2e-16). The data demonstrate that most genes with shared active enhancers are downregulated, indicating that active enhancer presence alone does not determine gene expression during transdifferentiation.

results.result: The vast majority of differentially methylated regions (DMRs) mapping to active enhancers in TFH and Tet+ cells are hypomethylated (92.5% and 88.7% respectively, p<2.2e-16), with most differentially methylated enhancers shared between these cell types (65-66%), indicating that the methylation status of distal gene regulatory elements for TR1-specific genes is imprinted at the TFH stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C128, C130-C132 are supported by integrated analysis of methylation, ATACseq, and ChIPseq data (Figure 7A-B, Figure 6C) showing that DMRs at active enhancers are predominantly hypomethylated and shared between TFH and Tet+ cells. The Il10 locus example (Figure 6C) demonstrates that genes upregulated at the TR1 stage have already demethylated their distal regulatory elements at the TFH stage, supporting the concept of epigenetic imprinting.

results.result: Transdifferentiation of TFH cells into TR1 cells is likely driven by changes in the expression of TFH-stabilizing and TR1-promoting transcription factors, possibly in response to sustained TCR ligation.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is supported by the comprehensive epigenetic data showing that TR1 genes are already poised for expression at the TFH stage, combined with previous work (cited) demonstrating that pMHCII-NPs trigger sustained TCR signaling. The observation that differential gene expression is dissociated from epigenetic changes, coupled with the finding that TF gene downregulation is associated with chromatin closure, supports the conclusion that changes in TF expression drive transdifferentiation.

results.result: Single-cell multiome analysis reveals distinct TFH and TR1 cell clusters, with the pMHCII-NP-induced TFH cells overlapping with KLH-induced effector TFH.1 cells (Bcl6hiTox2hiIl21+Pdcd1+), and these cell populations being more similar to each other than to other subsets despite arising from different stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55, C58 are supported by scMultiome data (Figure 1A-B) showing cell clustering and hierarchical analysis. The data demonstrate that pMHCII-NP-induced TFH cells and KLH-induced TFH.1 cells have overlapping transcriptional and epigenetic profiles, validating the use of KLH-induced TFH cells as a comparison for studying the TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process.

results.result: Bulk ATACseq analyses replicate single-cell findings, showing that KLH-induced TFH cells have 13-fold more differential OCRs than Tet+ cells, with 97.9% of Tet+ OCRs also present in TFH cells, and differential OCRs being significantly associated with gene upregulation (p<7.88e-11).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71, C73 are supported by bulk ATACseq and RNAseq data (Figure 2A-B) that faithfully replicate the scMultiome observations. The data provide independent validation of the chromatin closure phenomenon and its association with gene expression changes, strengthening the conclusions drawn from single-cell analyses.

results.result: H3K4me3 histone marks show similar overall deposition patterns between TFH and Tet+ cells, with only 123 differentially marked peaks between these cell types, and 77.6% of H3K4me3 peaks in genes with shared OCRs being present in all three cell types (TFH, Tet+, Tconv).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 are supported by H3K4me3 ChIPseq data (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1-3) showing minimal differences in H3K4me3 deposition between TFH and Tet+ cells. The data demonstrate that genes remaining open during transdifferentiation have nearly identical H3K4me3 landscapes, supporting the concept of epigenetic poising at the TFH stage.

results.result: H3K27me3 repressive marks show similar patterns between TFH and Tet+ cells, with only 167 differentially marked regions, and 95.8% of H3K27me3 marks in genes with shared OCRs being present in all three cell types, indicating these genes already had this mark at the naïve and TFH stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by H3K27me3 ChIPseq data (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1-3) showing that despite TFH cells having significantly more H3K27me3 peaks overall (42,274 vs. 3,236 in Tet+), there are minimal differences in H3K27me3 deposition for genes with shared chromatin accessibility. This supports the conclusion that repressive marks are also imprinted at the TFH stage.

results.result: H3K27Ac active marks show similar overall deposition patterns between TFH and Tet+ cells (~44,000 marks per cell type), with only 7 differentially marked regions, and 73.8% of H3K27ac marks in genes with shared OCRs being present in both TFH and Tet+ but not Tconv cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by H3K27Ac ChIPseq data (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1-3) showing remarkably similar H3K27ac deposition between TFH and Tet+ cells. Unlike H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, most H3K27ac marks in genes with shared OCRs were acquired at the TFH stage rather than being present in naïve cells, supporting the concept of active enhancer establishment during TFH differentiation.

results.result: DNA methylation analysis reveals that 43.2% of differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are shared between TFH and Tet+ cells, with 70-71% of genes with differential methylation in Tet+ cells also being differentially methylated in TFH cells, primarily in intronic CpG islands.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are supported by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing extensive sharing of methylation patterns between TFH and Tet+ cells. The statistical significance (p<2.2e-16) and high percentage of shared DMRs support the conclusion that TFH and Tet+ cells have remarkably similar methylomes.

results.result: Among genes with accessible chromatin in both TFH and TR1 cells, 328 of 545 harbor DMRs, with 87.5% having similar methylation status in both TFH and Tet+ cells (p<1.85e-5), and 48.5% being differentially expressed between TR1 and TFH cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are supported by integrated methylation and scMultiome data (Figure 4D) showing that genes remaining accessible during transdifferentiation share an even greater degree of methylation similarity than all genes. The lack of correlation between methylation status and differential expression (p=0.92) supports the conclusion that methylation is imprinted at the TFH stage but does not directly regulate differential expression.

results.result: Specific examples of methylation patterns show that Il2 (TFH-specific) and Il10 (TR1-specific) are both hypomethylated in TFH and Tet+ cells compared to Tconv, with only minor differences between TFH and Tet+ cells, while Il21 (expressed by both) is hypomethylated in both subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107, C110 are supported by detailed methylation analysis of specific loci (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing that even genes with differential expression between TFH and TR1 cells have similar methylation patterns. The data provide specific examples supporting the general conclusion that methylation status is imprinted at the TFH stage, with only minor changes during transdifferentiation.

results.result: Previous work has established that pMHCII-NP therapy triggers TFH cell expansion and transdifferentiation into TR1 cells that resolve autoimmune inflammation, with this process requiring Bcl6 and Irf4 for both TFH expansion and TR1 formation, while Prdm1 (Blimp-1) selectively gates the TFH-to-TR1 conversion.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C19 summarize previous work by the authors (cited references) that established the TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation pathway. These claims provide essential context for the current study and are supported by the cited literature. The current manuscript builds on this foundation by investigating the epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process.

results.result: BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-specific CD4+ T-cells are autoreactive T-cells contributing to type 1 diabetes in NOD mice, and treatment with cognate pMHCII-NPs leads to expansion of anti-diabetogenic TR1 cells and reversal of diabetes, with the induced Tet+ cell pools containing ~30% TFH and ~70% TR1 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 describe the experimental system used in the study and are supported by cited previous work and the current data. These claims establish the biological relevance of the model system and provide context for the cell populations analyzed in the epigenetic studies.

results.result: KLH-induced TFH.2 cells express lower levels of Pdcd1, Il21, Bcl6, and Tox2 and higher levels of Maf, Tcf7, Cxcr5, and Cd69 compared to TFH.1 cells, while TFH.3 cells display transcriptomic features of follicular T-regulatory cells (Foxp3+Bcl6+Bhlhe40+Icos+Il10+).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 describe the heterogeneity within the KLH-induced TFH population and are supported by cited previous work. These claims provide important context for understanding the TFH cell populations used as comparators in the epigenetic analyses, though they are not central to the main findings of the current study.

results.result: The hypothesis tested in this study is that pMHCII-NP-induced conversion of TFH cells into TR1 cells involves epigenetic re-programming of the TFH precursors.
results.evaluation: Claim C20 states the initial hypothesis of the study. However, the comprehensive epigenetic data presented actually refute this hypothesis, showing instead that TR1 genes are already epigenetically marked at the TFH stage rather than undergoing extensive epigenetic reprogramming. The study's findings demonstrate that transdifferentiation occurs through changes in TF expression rather than epigenetic reprogramming, making this hypothesis unsupported by the data.

results.result: Background knowledge establishes that chromatin modifications, histone modifications, and DNA methylation regulate T-cell differentiation, activation, and memory responses, with extensive epigenetic remodeling typically accompanying acquisition of new functional states by peripheral T-cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C21-C42 summarize established knowledge about epigenetic regulation of T-cell differentiation and function, supported by numerous cited references. These claims provide essential background context for understanding why the findings of the current study (showing minimal epigenetic changes during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation) are surprising and significant.

results.result: The TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process involves massive closure of open chromatin regions (OCRs), with most OCRs remaining open in TR1 cells already being accessible at the TFH stage, and minimal generation of new OCRs during the transition.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states the study 'effectively demonstrates that the TFH-to-TR1 differentiation process is associated with massive closure of OCRs.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'observations from different epigenetic perspectives mutually supported each other' and highlights this as a key finding. No concerns were raised about the chromatin accessibility data.

results.result: TR1-associated genes, including Il10, are already epigenetically poised for expression at the TFH cell stage, with accessible chromatin, hypomethylation, and active enhancer marks (H3K27ac) already in place, indicating that TFH cells are epigenetically primed to become TR1 cells.
results.evaluation: This central conclusion is strongly supported by all reviewers. The editor notes 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling' and Reviewer 1 states 'the authors successfully demonstrated that the TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation process is driven by pre-existing epigenetic modifications.' Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'the TR1-poised epigenome of TFH cells is a key enabler of this transdifferentiation process' as effectively demonstrated.

results.result: During the TFH-to-TR1 transition, 87.2% of differentially expressed genes are downregulated while only 12.8% are upregulated, with chromatin closure strongly associated with gene downregulation (94% of genes in closed chromatin regions are downregulated).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'their evidence indicated that the downregulation of TFH-related genes during the TFH to TR1 transition depends on chromatin closure, while the upregulation of TR1-related genes does not depend on epigenetic changes.' This finding is presented as a strength with no concerns raised about the data or interpretation.

results.result: Histone modification patterns (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, and H3K27ac) are nearly identical between TFH and TR1 cells for genes that remain accessible during the transition, with very few differentially marked regions between the two cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 highlights 'the use of high-throughput sequencing technologies and sophisticated bioinformatics analyses strengthens the foundation for the conclusions drawn.' Reviewer 2 notes that 'observations from different epigenetic perspectives mutually supported each other, lending greater credibility to their conclusions.' No concerns were raised about the histone modification data.

results.result: BDC2.5mi/I-Ag7-NP-induced Tet+ cells and KLH-induced TFH cells share remarkably similar DNA methylation patterns, with 87.5% of genes accessible in both TFH and TR1 cells having similar methylation status, and no correlation between methylation status and differential gene expression.
results.evaluation: The comprehensive methylation analysis is affirmed by reviewers as part of the 'detailed and comprehensive assessment of epigenetics' (Reviewer 2). The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling, supported by comprehensive transcriptional and epigenetic analyses.' No concerns were raised about the methylation data or its interpretation.

results.result: Active enhancers (marked by H3K27ac and open chromatin) linked to TR1-upregulated genes are predominantly hypomethylated and already present in TFH cells (89.6% shared), with no significant correlation between active enhancer distribution and differential gene expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes 'observations from different epigenetic perspectives mutually supported each other' and confirms the study demonstrates 'the TR1-poised epigenome of TFH cells is a key enabler of this transdifferentiation process.' The integration of multiple epigenetic marks is highlighted as a strength by Reviewer 1.

results.result: Active enhancers linked to TR1-upregulated genes are enriched for binding sites of TFH-associated transcription factors TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF, with ~61% of these TF-binding active enhancers already present in TFH cells, suggesting these sites are occupied at the TFH stage.
results.evaluation: This finding is part of the comprehensive epigenetic analysis affirmed by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes 'the identification of key transcription factors and epigenetic marks is a strong foundation for future work.' No concerns were raised about the transcription factor binding site analysis or its interpretation.

results.result: Bulk ATACseq analysis shows KLH-induced TFH cells have 13 times more differential OCRs than pMHCII-NP-induced Tet+ cells (10,919 vs. 821), with 97.9% of Tet+ differential OCRs also found in TFH cells, faithfully replicating single-cell observations.
results.evaluation: While Reviewer 2 acknowledges the bulk and single-cell data validate each other, they raise a significant concern: 'differential OCRs between Tet+ and naïve T cells were limited to only 821, as compared to 10,919 differential OCRs between KLH-TFH and naïve T cells...indicating that the precursors and T cell clonotypes that responded to pMHC-NP were extremely limited.' This limitation 'significantly limits the relevance of their conclusion to a broader perspective,' though the authors have discussed this in the revised manuscript.

results.result: Specific examples of differential methylation include Il10 (hypomethylated in TFH cells despite not being expressed), Il2 (hypomethylated in both TFH and Tet+ cells), and in some cases further demethylation of TR1-specific genes or remethylation of TFH-specific genes occurs during the transition.
results.evaluation: These specific examples support the broader methylation findings and are part of the comprehensive dataset affirmed by reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'a comprehensive epigenomic database of pMHC-NP induced TR1 cells' that 'will serve as a valuable reference for future research.' No concerns were raised about these specific gene examples.

results.result: Downregulated transcription factor-coding genes during TFH-to-TR1 conversion close significantly more OCRs (13/29) compared to upregulated TF genes (4/38), while upregulation of TF-coding genes is largely dissociated from the epigenetic marks studied.
results.evaluation: This finding is consistent with the overall conclusion that downregulation depends on chromatin closure while upregulation does not depend on new epigenetic changes, as affirmed by Reviewer 2. The comprehensive nature of the analysis is highlighted as a strength by all reviewers.

results.result: Transdifferentiation of TFH cells into TR1 cells is likely driven by changes in expression of TFH-stabilizing and TR1-promoting transcription factors, possibly in response to sustained TCR ligation.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation is accepted by reviewers as a reasonable conclusion from the data. Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors are actively investigating how these factors drive chromatin remodeling, which will enhance the mechanistic understanding' in future studies, indicating acceptance of the current interpretation while acknowledging room for further mechanistic work.

results.result: Single-cell multiome analysis reveals distinct TFH subpopulations (TFH.1, TFH.2, TFH.3) with pMHCII-NP-induced TFH cells overlapping with KLH-induced TFH.1 effector cells, and hierarchical clustering confirms transcriptional and epigenetic similarity between these populations despite different origins.
results.evaluation: The single-cell analysis is part of the comprehensive approach praised by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 states 'the study employs a broad range of bulk and single-cell transcriptional and epigenetic tools...this comprehensive approach provides a detailed examination.' No concerns were raised about the cell clustering or characterization.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the finding of massive chromatin closure during TFH-to-TR1 transdifferentiation (C4, C44, C59-C61, C68, C139-C140). OpenEval emphasizes the consistency between scMultiome and bulk ATACseq data, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding with no concerns raised. OpenEval includes C5 which peer review addresses separately.

Both support the association between chromatin closure and gene downregulation (C62-C65). OpenEval provides statistical evidence (p=8.25e-14, p=1.38e-08) from scRNAseq and bulk analyses. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm that downregulation of TFH-related genes depends on chromatin closure, presented as a strength with no concerns.

Both support epigenetic poising at the TFH stage (C6, C8, C45, C47, C94, C141). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive epigenetic analyses showing nearly identical patterns. Peer reviewers strongly affirm this central conclusion, with the editor noting 'compelling evidence' and Reviewer 1 confirming successful demonstration of pre-existing epigenetic modifications. OpenEval addresses additional claims not in peer result.

Both support methylation imprinting at the TFH stage (C7, C46, C99, C108, C142). OpenEval provides specific statistical evidence (87.5% similarity, p<1.85e-5) from bisulfite sequencing. Peer reviewers affirm the comprehensive methylation analysis as part of the 'detailed and comprehensive assessment of epigenetics' with no concerns raised.

Both support the finding that transcription factor binding sites are established at the TFH stage (C9, C133-C137). OpenEval provides quantitative data showing 34.4-70.1% of active enhancers have TOX-2, IRF4, and c-MAF binding sites. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the comprehensive epigenetic analysis, with Reviewer 1 noting the identification of key transcription factors as a strong foundation.

Both support the main conclusion that genomic imprinting enables transdifferentiation (C10, C48, C138, C144). OpenEval emphasizes integration of all epigenetic data. Peer reviewers strongly affirm this central conclusion, with all three reviewers confirming the evidence is compelling and the TR1-poised epigenome is effectively demonstrated as a key enabler.

Both support the dissociation between differential gene expression and epigenetic marks (C66-C67, C104, C109, C111-C112, C119, C122, C129). OpenEval provides statistical evidence (p=0.92, p=0.76, p=1) showing no significant correlations. Peer reviewers affirm the comprehensive methylation analysis with no concerns, though they address this finding more broadly across multiple results.

Perfect agreement on claims C114-C115. Both support that TF gene downregulation is driven by chromatin closure while TR1-promoting TF upregulation occurs independently. OpenEval provides statistical evidence (p<0.0001) from integrated scMultiome and epigenetic data. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm this finding as effectively demonstrated.

Both support findings about active enhancer sharing and its dissociation from gene expression (C116-C118, C120-C121). OpenEval shows 80.2% vs 55.5% sharing (p<2.2e-16) and notes most genes with shared enhancers are downregulated. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the mutually supporting observations from different epigenetic perspectives.

Both support the finding that DMRs at active enhancers are predominantly hypomethylated and shared (C123-C128, C130-C132). OpenEval uses the Il10 locus as a key example. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the comprehensive epigenetic analysis demonstrating the TR1-poised epigenome, with observations from different perspectives mutually supporting each other.

Perfect agreement on claim C145. Both support the mechanistic conclusion that changes in TF expression drive transdifferentiation. OpenEval integrates comprehensive epigenetic data with previous work on sustained TCR signaling. Peer reviewers accept this interpretation as reasonable, with Reviewer 1 noting future mechanistic work will enhance understanding.

Both support the validation of the experimental system (C53-C55, C58). OpenEval emphasizes overlapping transcriptional and epigenetic profiles between pMHCII-NP-induced TFH and KLH-induced TFH.1 cells. Peer reviewers praise the comprehensive single-cell approach with no concerns about cell clustering or characterization. OpenEval does not address C56-C57 which peer review includes.

Both address bulk ATACseq validation (C69-C70, C73). OpenEval emphasizes faithful replication of scMultiome observations. However, peer reviewers raise a significant concern about limited differential OCRs (821 vs 10,919), indicating extremely limited precursors responding to pMHC-NP, which 'significantly limits the relevance of their conclusion to a broader perspective.' This represents a notable divergence in evaluation.

Both support H3K4me3 findings showing minimal differences between TFH and Tet+ cells (C76-C82). OpenEval emphasizes nearly identical H3K4me3 landscapes for genes remaining open. Peer reviewers affirm the histone modification data as part of the sophisticated bioinformatics analyses strengthening conclusions, with observations from different perspectives mutually supporting each other.

Both support H3K27me3 findings showing minimal differences for genes with shared chromatin accessibility (C83-C88). OpenEval notes the paradox of more overall peaks in TFH (42,274 vs 3,236) but similar patterns for shared genes. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the comprehensive histone modification analysis with no concerns raised.

Both support H3K27ac findings showing similar deposition between TFH and Tet+ cells (C89-C93). OpenEval notes most marks were acquired at TFH stage rather than present in naïve cells. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the comprehensive epigenetic analysis, with different perspectives mutually supporting conclusions.

Both support extensive sharing of methylation patterns between TFH and Tet+ cells (C95-C98). OpenEval provides statistical evidence (p<2.2e-16) from whole-genome bisulfite sequencing. Peer reviewers affirm the comprehensive methylation analysis as part of the detailed epigenetic assessment with no concerns raised.

Both support that genes remaining accessible share greater methylation similarity (C100-C103). OpenEval emphasizes lack of correlation between methylation and differential expression (p=0.92). Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the comprehensive methylation dataset that will serve as a valuable reference for future research.

Perfect agreement on claims C105-C107, C110. Both support that specific loci show similar methylation despite differential expression. OpenEval provides detailed examples from Figure 4 supplement 2. Peer reviewers affirm these examples as part of the comprehensive dataset with no concerns raised.

OpenEval evaluates claims about the experimental system (C49-C52) as supported by cited previous work and current data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers generally affirm the experimental approach.

Both address KLH-induced TFH heterogeneity (C56-C57). OpenEval notes these claims provide context from previous work but are not central to current findings. Peer reviewers include these in their affirmation of the single-cell analysis and comprehensive approach with no concerns raised.
